history.heading: Dilmun
paragraphs: Bahrain, an archipelago in the Persian Gulf, was the centre of the ancient civilisation of Dilmun, a trading hub between Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley from around 3000 BCE. Thousands of ancient burial mounds remain, and Qal'at al-Bahrain, a site inhabited for millennia, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The islands were later influenced by Assyrians, Babylonians, Greeks (who called them Tylos) and Persians, and adopted Islam in the 7th century.

history.heading: Portuguese, Persians and the Al Khalifa
paragraphs: The Portuguese controlled Bahrain in the 16th century, followed by Persian rule. In 1783 the Al Khalifa family, from the Arabian Peninsula, took control and still rules today.
In the 19th century Bahrain signed treaties with Britain and became a British protectorate. Pearl diving was the backbone of the economy until the 1930s.

history.heading: Oil and independence
paragraphs: In 1932 Bahrain became the first place on the Arab side of the Gulf where oil was discovered. It became independent from Britain in 1971 after Iran dropped its claim to the islands.

In 2011 large protests, mainly by the Shia majority, demanded political reforms; they were suppressed with support from Saudi and Emirati forces. In 2020 Bahrain normalised relations with Israel under the Abraham Accords.

culture.heading: Society and traditions
paragraphs: Arabic is the official language, and English is widely used. Islam is the state religion; Bahraini citizens include a Shia majority and a Sunni minority, which includes the ruling family. A large share of the population consists of foreign workers, many from South Asia.

Traditional culture includes pearl-diving songs, Arabian horses and falconry, and the Pearling Trail in Muharraq is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Machboos, spiced rice with meat or fish, is the national dish. Bahrain hosts a Formula One Grand Prix.

politics.heading: Constitutional monarchy
paragraphs: Bahrain is a constitutional monarchy headed by a king, who holds wide powers and appoints the government. The National Assembly has an elected Council of Representatives and an appointed Consultative Council.

Main opposition groups have been dissolved since the 2011 unrest, and human rights organisations criticise restrictions on political activity. Bahrain hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet and is closely allied with Saudi Arabia, to which it is linked by the King Fahd Causeway.

economy.heading: Beyond oil
paragraphs: Bahrain has smaller oil reserves than its Gulf neighbours and was the first to diversify. It is a regional centre for banking, including Islamic finance, and has a large aluminium smelter, Alba, as well as tourism and logistics.

Oil still provides most government revenue, and public debt is high, requiring support from Gulf allies. There is no personal income tax. The currency is the Bahraini dinar, one of the most valuable currency units in the world.
